name: Image Editor
title: Image Editor — Crop, Adjust and Annotate Locally
description: Crop, rotate and flip photos, adjust brightness, contrast and colour, add a text overlay, then export PNG, JPG or WebP — all locally in your browser.
intro: A compact photo editor for the tweaks you need most: straighten a crop, correct exposure, add a caption and save in a web-friendly format. Everything happens in your browser, so your original file never leaves the device. There is no account, upload queue or waiting step.
instructions: Upload a JPG, PNG or WebP image from your device.
Drag the crop slider to trim edges and set the frame you want.
Use rotate and flip controls to get the orientation right.
Apply brightness, contrast, saturation, blur, grayscale or sepia adjustments.
Add and position a text overlay, then preview the result.
Choose PNG, JPG or WebP and download the finished image.

example.input: 2400×1600 JPEG with a skewed horizon and no caption
example.output: 1600×1200 PNG with a straightened crop and caption text

faqs.q: Is my photo uploaded anywhere?
faqs.a: No. The image is decoded and edited by JavaScript running in your browser. Nothing is sent to LetitEdit or to a third-party image service, and closing the page clears the working copy.

faqs.q: What can I actually change here?
faqs.a: You can crop with a slider, rotate and flip, adjust brightness, contrast, saturation and blur, apply grayscale or sepia, and add a text overlay. It is meant for quick corrections rather than layered design work.

faqs.q: Which formats can I export?
faqs.a: PNG, JPG and WebP. PNG keeps sharp text and flat colour, JPG produces smaller photo files, and WebP offers a good size and quality balance where it is supported.

faqs.q: Why does my export look different from the preview?
faqs.a: JPG and WebP are lossy, so fine gradients or small text can soften slightly after saving. Choose PNG when you need pixel-exact output, and re-check the preview after changing format.

faqs.q: This tool feels slow with a large photo. What can I do?
faqs.a: Very high-resolution files can take a moment to process in any browser. Crop first to reduce the working area, close other heavy tabs, and try a smaller source image if the page becomes unresponsive.

article.heading: A lightweight editor for everyday photos
paragraphs: Most photo jobs are small: a crooked horizon, a dim exposure, a caption that needs to sit in the corner. This editor collects those everyday corrections in one place so you can finish them without installing software or handing a file to a remote service. You load an image, trim it with a crop slider, fix the orientation with rotate and flip, then tune brightness, contrast and saturation until the picture looks right. Blur, grayscale and sepia are available for stylistic changes, and a text overlay lets you label a screenshot or mark up a shared photo. The preview updates as you work, so each adjustment is easy to judge before you commit. When you are satisfied, you download the result in PNG, JPG or WebP. The original file on your device is never modified.

article.heading: The workflow from upload to export
paragraphs: Start by uploading a JPG, PNG or WebP image from your device. The editor decodes it locally and places it in the preview area. Next, drag the crop slider to choose how much of the frame to keep; cropping early reduces the area that later filters have to process. If the picture is sideways or mirrored, apply rotate or flip before anything else, because text and colour decisions are easier once the orientation is correct. Then work through the adjustments in small steps rather than pushing a single slider to its limit. Add a text overlay last, position it over a clear part of the image, and check that it remains readable. Finally, pick an export format and download. If a result disappoints you, reset the adjustments and try again.

article.heading: Understanding the adjustments
paragraphs: Brightness lifts or lowers the overall lightness of every pixel, which helps with an underexposed shot but can wash out highlights if pushed too far. Contrast widens or narrows the gap between light and dark tones, making a flat image look punchier. Saturation controls the intensity of colour; reducing it moves a photo toward grayscale, while increasing it can make skies and clothing look unnaturally vivid. Blur softens detail and is useful for de-emphasising a busy background, though it cannot recover information that is out of focus. Grayscale removes colour entirely, and sepia applies a warm brown tint for an older look. These controls are deliberately simple, so combine them gently and compare against the original preview rather than trusting a single number.

article.heading: Choosing the right export format
paragraphs: PNG is lossless, which means it preserves the exact pixels you see in the preview. Choose it when your overlay contains small text, sharp lines or flat colour, because compression artefacts are most visible around lettering. JPG is lossy and produces much smaller files for photographs with smooth gradients and natural texture; it is a good default for sharing a photo where a few extra kilobytes matter. WebP sits between the two in many cases, offering efficient compression and support for transparency in current browsers. If a downloaded file looks softer than the preview, switch to PNG and compare again. Remember that re-saving a JPG a second time adds another generation of loss, so keep an original copy and export from that rather than from a previous download.

article.heading: Privacy, limits and troubleshooting
paragraphs: Editing happens in your browser, so your photo is not uploaded to a server and no account is required. That also means the page cannot reach files stored elsewhere in your cloud drive unless you download them first. This is a single-image editor for quick corrections, not a layer-based design application: there are no masks, brush tools or undo history beyond what the preview offers. Very large files may take longer to decode and render, especially on older devices. If the page becomes sluggish, crop the image first, close other tabs and retry with a smaller file. If an overlay disappears or a slider seems to have no effect, reset the tool and reload the image, then apply changes one at a time so you can see which step causes the problem.

name: HEIC Viewer & Converter
title: HEIC Viewer & Converter — Open and Convert HEIF Images
description: Open .heic and .heif photos in your browser, preview one or many files and download PNG or JPG copies. Decoding uses a local library; no files are uploaded.
intro: View Apple-style HEIC and HEIF photos without installing a desktop converter. Load a single image or a whole batch, inspect real previews and download PNG or JPG copies. Files are decoded in your browser with a locally loaded libheif library.
instructions: Choose one or more .heic or .heif files from your device.
Wait while the local decoder generates previews; large batches take longer.
Click a thumbnail to inspect the decoded image at a larger size.
Pick PNG or JPG as the download format for each image or the batch.
Review any failure messages and skip files the decoder cannot read.

example.output: IMG_0042.png preview plus a 4032×3024 PNG download

faqs.q: Are my HEIC photos uploaded to a server?
faqs.a: No. The viewer loads a libheif decoder library locally and decodes files in your browser. Your photos are not sent to LetitEdit or to any conversion service.

faqs.q: Why won't my file open?
faqs.a: HEIC files can use different codecs and some variants are not supported by the current browser decoder. If decoding fails, the tool reports the failure rather than showing a blank or fake preview. Try exporting the photo as JPEG from the source device.

faqs.q: Can I convert many files at once?
faqs.a: Yes. Batch mode accepts multiple .heic and .heif files, shows a thumbnail for each decoded image and lets you download PNG or JPG copies. Files the decoder cannot read are listed as failures instead of being silently skipped.

faqs.q: Which output format should I choose?
faqs.a: PNG is lossless and keeps the decoded pixels exactly, which suits screenshots and graphics. JPG is smaller and is usually better for photographs. Neither adds information that was not in the original HEIC file.

faqs.q: Why does conversion take a while?
faqs.a: HEIC uses efficient compression, so decoding is more work than opening a JPEG. A batch of high-resolution photos can take noticeable time even on a fast machine. Keep the tab active and wait for the status message before downloading.

article.heading: Why HEIC needs a real decoder
paragraphs: Photos from many modern phones are saved in HEIC or HEIF format, which uses more efficient compression than JPEG. That efficiency is useful on a device with limited storage, but it also means a browser cannot simply display the file the way it displays a JPEG. This viewer loads a libheif decoder library locally and uses it to turn each file into pixels the page can show. The result is a genuine preview generated from your photo, not a placeholder or an icon. If decoding fails, the tool says so plainly instead of inventing a successful result. You can then decide whether to retry, convert the file on the source device or use the successfully decoded images in the batch. If you depend on these pictures regularly, keeping the original files alongside converted copies saves you repeating the step later.

article.heading: Viewing a single photo
paragraphs: For one image, choose the .heic or .heif file and wait for the decoder to finish. A thumbnail appears once the file is read, and selecting it opens a larger preview. This preview is useful for checking orientation, colour and whether the photo you picked is the one you wanted before you spend time downloading a converted copy. HEIC stores more than just pixels — some files carry depth maps, live-photo pairs or multiple representations — and the viewer shows the primary still image. Extra payloads are not exposed as separate downloads. If the preview looks empty or the status area shows an error, the decoder could not interpret that particular file; the page will not quietly present a blank image as a success. Try another file to confirm the viewer itself is working before you investigate the source.

article.heading: Converting a batch
paragraphs: Batch mode is the practical choice when you have moved a folder of photos off a phone. Select several files at once and the viewer decodes them one by one, listing a thumbnail for each success and an error for each failure. Choose PNG or JPG for the downloads. PNG keeps the decoded pixels without further loss and is a good fit for graphics or images with sharp edges, while JPG produces smaller files that are easier to email or upload. Mixed results are normal: a folder can contain both standard HEIC files and variants that the current decoder cannot handle. Failed items are reported by name so you can deal with them separately instead of wondering which conversions quietly disappeared. Work through the failures after the successful files are downloaded.

article.heading: Formats, quality and file size
paragraphs: Converting HEIC to PNG or JPG is a change of container and compression, not an enhancement. The decoder reconstructs the pixels that were stored in the HEIC file; the encoder then writes them into the format you chose. PNG preserves those pixels exactly and can produce a large file, especially for a high-resolution phone photo. JPG compresses again, which reduces size but can introduce slight softness around fine detail. Neither format restores motion in a live-photo pair or reveals detail that was never captured. If you need a smaller result for a website, convert first and then resize or compress with a dedicated tool. Keep the original HEIC file as your master copy so you can re-convert later with different settings.

article.heading: Privacy and troubleshooting
paragraphs: All decoding and encoding happens in your browser. The viewer uses a locally loaded libheif library, and your photos are not uploaded to LetitEdit or to a third-party conversion service. That is reassuring for personal pictures, but it also means the page depends on your browser's capabilities. Very large batches can be slow, so keep the tab active and wait for each status message before leaving. If a file fails, check that the extension really is .heic or .heif, then try re-exporting it from the source device as JPEG and see whether that copy opens. Older browsers may lack features the decoder needs; updating the browser often fixes unexplained failures. Should the page become unresponsive, reload it and process the photos in smaller groups.

name: Add Border to Image
title: Add Border to Image — Adjustable Solid Colour Frame
description: Wrap a photo in a solid colour border of any width and colour. Preview the frame live, keep the original image intact and download the bordered result as a PNG.
intro: Add a clean, adjustable frame around a single image without opening a design program. Choose the border width and a solid colour, watch the preview update and download a PNG that contains the original picture plus the frame you set.
instructions: Upload one image from your device.
Set the border width to the thickness you want.
Pick a solid colour for the frame.
Check the preview to confirm the frame sits evenly around the picture.
Download the bordered PNG; the original file stays unchanged.

faqs.q: Does the image leave my device?
faqs.a: No. The border is drawn in your browser with canvas, and the file is never uploaded to LetitEdit or another service. Your original image is not modified.

faqs.q: Can I use different colours on each side?
faqs.a: No. This tool adds a single solid colour border of equal width on all four sides. For multiple colours or uneven frames you need a full graphic editor.

faqs.q: What happens at the image edges?
faqs.a: The border is added outside the original pixels, so nothing is cropped or covered. The downloaded PNG is wider and taller than the input by twice the border width.

faqs.q: Why is my downloaded file a PNG?
faqs.a: PNG keeps the solid colour edges crisp and avoids compression smudging around the frame, so it is the export format for this tool.

faqs.q: The border looks thin or invisible. What should I check?
faqs.a: Increase the width value; a few pixels can be hard to see on a large preview. Also check that the chosen colour contrasts with the image edge, because a white frame on a white background is easy to miss.

article.heading: What the border tool does
paragraphs: A border tool solves a small but common problem: a photo needs a little space around it before it is posted, printed or placed on a slide. This one takes a single image and draws a solid colour frame around the outside of the original pixels. You set the width in pixels and choose one colour, and the preview shows exactly how the finished picture will look. Because the frame is added outside the image rather than painted over it, no part of your photo is covered or trimmed. The download is a new PNG file that contains both the original content and the frame. The file you uploaded stays untouched on your device, so you can try several colours or widths without losing the source. If you are preparing several versions, keep the original handy and export each variant separately.

article.heading: A quick workflow
paragraphs: Upload one image to begin. The tool reads it locally and shows it in the preview area. Move the width control until the frame looks proportionate to the picture — a thick border can suit a small icon, while a large photo often needs only a slim edge. Next choose a solid colour. Neutral black or white is safe for most uses, but a colour sampled from the photo can look considered. Watch the preview as you adjust both settings, because the same width looks different on a small thumbnail and a large image. When the frame looks right, download the PNG. If you want to compare options, change the colour or width and download a second copy; each export is independent and the original file is never overwritten.

article.heading: Choosing width and colour
paragraphs: Border width is measured in pixels, so its visual impact depends on the size of the image. On an 800-pixel-wide photo, a 20-pixel frame is a modest outline; on a 200-pixel avatar, the same setting dominates. Think about where the result will appear: a frame that looks balanced on a desktop preview may disappear in a social-media thumbnail. Colour matters just as much. A high-contrast frame separates the photo from a busy page, while a subtle tone lets the image speak for itself. Since the border is a single solid colour, avoid expecting gradients, patterns or separate colours per side. If you need those effects, a screenshot beautifier or a full design tool is a better fit.

article.heading: Why the output is PNG
paragraphs: The tool exports PNG because it keeps the frame edges clean. A lossy format such as JPG would introduce faint blocking around the boundary between the solid colour and the photograph, which is exactly where a crisp edge matters most. PNG stores the pixels directly, so the colour stays even and the transition remains sharp. The trade-off is file size: a bordered PNG can be larger than a comparable JPG, especially for a photo with lots of detail. If size matters more than edge quality, you can run the downloaded file through an image compressor afterwards. Remember that adding a border increases the canvas dimensions by twice the border width in each direction, so a 50-pixel frame adds 100 pixels to both the width and the height.

article.heading: Privacy and troubleshooting
paragraphs: All drawing happens in your browser, and the image is not uploaded anywhere. That makes the tool convenient for pictures you would rather not send to a remote service. If the border seems too thin, increase the width and check the preview again; a handful of pixels can be nearly invisible on a high-resolution display. If the frame appears to blend into the page, pick a colour with stronger contrast against what surrounds the picture. A frame that looks uneven is usually an optical effect caused by a very wide border on a small image, so try reducing it. Very large photos can take a moment to render; wait for the preview to settle before downloading, and reload the page if it stops responding. You can also try a different source format if one particular file never renders correctly.

name: Photo Merger
title: Photo Merger — Combine Images Horizontally or Vertically
description: Join up to six images into one picture, side by side or stacked, with adjustable spacing and a single PNG download. The merge happens locally in your browser.
intro: Combine several photos into a single image without a layout program. Choose a horizontal row or a vertical stack, add up to six files, set the gap between them and download one PNG. Everything runs in your browser.
instructions: Upload up to six images you want to combine.
Choose Horizontal or Vertical for the layout.
Set the spacing between neighbouring images.
Reorder files if needed so the result reads in the right sequence.
Preview the combined canvas, then download the PNG.

example.input: Three 600×400 JPEGs of the same subject

faqs.q: Are the uploaded photos stored or sent anywhere?
faqs.a: No. Images are read and drawn in your browser. They are not uploaded to LetitEdit or a third party, and closing the page discards the working copies.

faqs.q: How many images can I combine?
faqs.a: Up to six. The limit keeps the preview responsive and the resulting canvas manageable. For longer sequences, merge smaller groups and combine those results in a second pass.

faqs.q: What if my photos have different sizes?
faqs.a: The merger places images on a shared canvas without resizing them, so mismatched heights in a row or widths in a stack will be visible. Resize the files first if you need a uniform grid.

faqs.q: What does the spacing control do?
faqs.a: It sets the gap between neighbouring images on the final canvas. The background of that gap is transparent in the PNG, so placing the result on a coloured page will show the page colour between photos.

faqs.q: The download looks blank or incomplete. What went wrong?
faqs.a: Very large inputs can exceed what the browser can draw comfortably. Try fewer images, smaller source files or a smaller spacing value, wait for the preview to finish, then download again.

article.heading: When a single canvas is easier
paragraphs: Sometimes the clearest way to show several photos is to place them together on one canvas. A before-and-after pair, a three-step tutorial or a set of product angles all read better as a single image than as separate attachments. This tool does that one job: it takes up to six pictures and arranges them in a horizontal row or a vertical stack, with a gap you control. You do not need to learn layers or alignment guides. The preview shows the finished arrangement before you download anything, and the export is a PNG containing all the images on one transparent-backed canvas. Because the work happens in your browser, the photos never travel to a remote service. You can experiment with layouts freely, because nothing is saved until you download.

article.heading: Building a merged image
paragraphs: Start by uploading the images in the order you want them to appear. Most browsers let you select several files at once, but you can also check the order in the preview and rearrange if the tool offers that control. Next choose the layout. Horizontal places images left to right and is natural for comparisons and panoramas; vertical stacks them top to bottom and suits instructions or long screenshots. Then set the spacing. A small gap keeps the group tight, while a larger one gives each photo room to breathe. Watch the preview as you adjust — the canvas grows to fit the arrangement. When the sequence looks right, download the PNG. If something is wrong, change the layout or order and export again rather than trying to patch the file elsewhere.

article.heading: Spacing, sizes and alignment
paragraphs: The spacing value controls the gap between neighbouring images, not the margin around the outside of the canvas. That gap is transparent in the downloaded PNG, so its appearance depends on the background where you place the result. On a white page it will look white; on a dark page it will look dark. The merger does not rescale your files. If you combine a tall portrait with a wide landscape in a row, their heights will differ and the shorter one will sit against empty space. That is fine for some layouts and distracting for others. When you need an even grid, resize the source images to matching dimensions first, then merge them. A little preparation produces a much tidier result than trying to correct alignment after the fact.

article.heading: Formats and practical uses
paragraphs: PNG is the export format because it preserves the combined pixels exactly and supports transparency in the gaps. That makes the result easy to drop into a document, a slide or a webpage without a white box appearing around it. The input files can be common web formats such as JPG, PNG and WebP, provided your browser can decode them. Typical uses include side-by-side comparisons, multi-angle product shots, comic-style sequences and concatenated screenshots. For a very long vertical stack, consider whether the result will be viewed on a small screen; an extremely tall image can be awkward to scroll. Splitting it into shorter sections is often more readable than producing one giant file. Keep the source files together in a named folder so you can rebuild the arrangement later.

article.heading: Privacy, limits and troubleshooting
paragraphs: Merging runs locally in your browser, so your images are not uploaded and no account is needed. The practical limit is six files, which keeps rendering predictable. Large, high-resolution photos can still make the canvas heavy, so if the preview is slow or the download looks incomplete, reduce the number of images or resize them before merging. Check that every file actually decoded — a corrupt source can leave a blank area in the arrangement. If the gap looks wrong, remember it is transparent and check the page behind it. When the sequence appears in the wrong order, adjust the upload order and export again. Reloading the page clears the current set and gives you a clean start. If a particular file consistently fails to appear, replace that copy with a fresh export from its source.

name: Screenshot Beautifier
title: Screenshot Beautifier — Frames, Backgrounds and Shadows
description: Dress up a screenshot with gradient, solid, transparent or patterned backgrounds, padding, rounded corners, shadow, filters and title bars. Export a polished PNG.
intro: Turn a raw screenshot into something presentable in one pass. Add a background, padding, rounded corners and a soft shadow, apply a filter or a text overlay, and optionally frame the image with a Mac or Windows-style title bar. Download the finished PNG.
instructions: Upload the screenshot you want to present.
Choose a gradient, solid, transparent or pattern background.
Set padding, corner radius and shadow to frame the capture.
Apply a filter, add text or select a Mac/Windows-style title bar.
Preview the composition, then export it as a PNG.

example.input: 1440×900 Windows app screenshot with a plain white frame
example.output: 1600×1060 PNG with gradient background, rounded corners and shadow

faqs.q: Is my screenshot uploaded?
faqs.a: No. The composition is assembled in your browser, and the screenshot is never sent to LetitEdit or a third-party service.

faqs.q: Can I make the background transparent?
faqs.a: Yes. Choose the transparent background option when you want the padding around the screenshot to stay see-through in the exported PNG.

faqs.q: What do the Mac and Windows title bars do?
faqs.a: They add a decorative window bar above the capture with the familiar dot or button styling. They are visual framing only and do not change the screenshot content beneath.

faqs.q: Will this fix a blurry or low-resolution screenshot?
faqs.a: No. Filters and framing can make a capture look tidier, but they cannot add detail that was not captured. Start with the sharpest original you have.

faqs.q: My export has a hard edge or the shadow is cut off. Why?
faqs.a: Increase the padding so there is enough room around the screenshot for the shadow to render. Also check that a transparent background is not being viewed against a similarly coloured page.

article.heading: Why raw screenshots need a little work
paragraphs: A screenshot dropped straight into a document often looks accidental. Its edges butt against the page, the surrounding colours clash, and there is nothing to tell the eye where the capture begins. A beautifier addresses those presentation problems without asking you to open a design application. You load the image, choose a background for the space around it, add padding so it does not crowd the edges, and optionally soften the corners and add a drop shadow. Text and filters are available for emphasis, and a decorative title bar can make the capture look like a window. The result is a clean PNG that reads as deliberate rather than pasted in a hurry. The controls are live, so you can compare a few styles before committing to a download.

article.heading: Starting with the background
paragraphs: The background is the area behind and around your screenshot, and it sets the tone for everything else. A gradient gives a modern look and works well in presentations and social posts. A solid colour is predictable and easy to match to a brand palette or document theme. Transparent leaves the surrounding area see-through, which is useful when the result will be placed on a page that already has its own colour or texture. A pattern adds visual interest but can distract from dense text, so use it sparingly. Choose the background before fine-tuning padding and shadow, because those settings interact with what sits behind the image. A dark background, for example, makes a subtle shadow harder to see. If in doubt, start with a solid colour and switch to gradient or pattern once the framing is settled.

article.heading: Padding, corners and shadow
paragraphs: Padding is the space between the screenshot and the edge of the finished canvas. Even a modest amount gives the image breathing room and prevents it from looking cramped. Rounded corners soften the hard rectangle of a raw capture; a small radius reads as polished, while a large one can start to crop visual information at the corners. Shadow adds depth by separating the screenshot from the background, but it needs room to render — if the padding is too tight, the shadow gets cut off and looks like a hard edge. Tune these three controls together in the preview. Increase padding when the shadow disappears, reduce the radius if corners look clipped, and keep the overall effect subtle when the screenshot contains small text. Small adjustments are easier to judge than dramatic ones, especially when the capture includes fine lettering.

article.heading: Filters, text and title bars
paragraphs: Filters can shift the mood of a capture. A slight desaturation reduces visual noise, while a warmer or cooler tint can help the screenshot sit alongside other images. They are enhancements, not repairs: no filter recovers text that was captured at too low a resolution. A text overlay lets you label the image or point out a detail, but keep it short and place it where it will not cover important content. The Mac and Windows-style title bars are decorative frames with familiar dots or buttons above the capture. They make a screenshot look like a tidy window and are useful in documentation. They do not alter the application shown underneath, so do not treat them as evidence of a particular operating system. Place text in the padding area rather than over the interface whenever possible.

article.heading: Export, privacy and troubleshooting
paragraphs: The finished composition downloads as a PNG, which keeps edges, text and shadows crisp. Editing happens in your browser: the screenshot is not uploaded to LetitEdit or to any external service. If the exported image looks cropped, check the padding first, because a shadow needs space to fade out. If the background seems to vanish, you may have selected transparent and are viewing the PNG against a similarly coloured page. A title bar that looks oversized on a small capture can be left off without affecting the rest of the layout. Very large screenshots may take a moment to render; wait for the preview to settle before exporting. Reloading the page clears the current composition so you can start again. Keeping a copy of the original screenshot also lets you try a completely different style later.

name: Black & White Image Converter
title: Black & White Image Converter — Grayscale and Threshold Modes
description: Convert photos to black and white in your browser. Pick smooth grayscale or an adjustable threshold for line art, keep transparency, and export PNG, JPG or WebP.
intro: Convert a color image to black and white without uploading it. Use smooth grayscale for photographs or an adjustable threshold to turn sketches and scanned line art into crisp high-contrast shapes. Transparent areas stay transparent, and the result downloads as PNG, JPG or WebP.
instructions: Open a PNG, JPG or WebP image from your device.
Choose Grayscale for natural tones or Threshold for high-contrast line art.
Adjust the threshold slider until dark and light areas separate cleanly.
Preview the result and confirm transparent pixels remain transparent.
Download the image as PNG, JPG or WebP.

example.input: A color photo with a transparent background
example.output: A grayscale version with the same transparency, saved as PNG

faqs.q: Is my image uploaded anywhere?
faqs.a: No. The conversion runs in your browser using the image data you open. Nothing is sent to a server, and closing the page clears the working copy.

faqs.q: What is the difference between grayscale and threshold?
faqs.a: Grayscale maps each pixel to a shade of gray, keeping subtle detail. Threshold converts pixels to pure black or white based on a slider, which suits line art, stamps and text scans.

faqs.q: Will transparent pixels stay transparent?
faqs.a: Yes. Alpha values are left unchanged in both modes, so logos and cut-outs keep their soft edges. Choose PNG or WebP to preserve transparency; JPG does not support it.

faqs.q: Can it colorise or restore an old photograph?
faqs.a: No. It only removes color information. It cannot add color, repair scratches, straighten a skewed page or enlarge a small image.

faqs.q: Why does my threshold preview look too dark or too noisy?
faqs.a: Lighting and compression artifacts push pixels across the cut-off. Move the slider slowly, try grayscale first, and use a clean evenly lit scan for crisp line art. Large images may take a moment to render.

article.heading: What the converter does
paragraphs: A black and white conversion removes color information and keeps the brightness of each pixel. This tool does that work in your browser, so a photo, logo or scan never has to leave your device. Two modes cover the usual jobs: a smooth grayscale render for photographs and an adjustable threshold for artwork that should contain only pure black and white. You open an image, pick a mode, check the preview and download the result. Nothing is renamed or reordered, and no account is needed. Because the image is processed as pixels, the output keeps the same dimensions as the source unless you resize it elsewhere. The original file on disk is never changed, so you can compare versions side by side.

article.heading: Grayscale mode for photographs
paragraphs: Grayscale mode blends the red, green and blue channels into a single luminance value, producing a continuous range of gray tones. Skin, fabric, sky and shadows remain distinguishable because hundreds of shades are preserved. This is the right choice for portraits, landscapes and any picture where texture matters more than a stark graphic effect. The converter uses a weighted luminance calculation, so colors with the same brightness do not necessarily look identical afterward; a saturated red can become darker than a pale blue. If a photo looks flat in grayscale, try increasing contrast in an image editor first, then bring it back here for the final black and white pass. That weighting matches human perception better than a simple average.

article.heading: Threshold mode for line art
paragraphs: Threshold mode reduces every pixel to one of two values. A slider sets the cut-off: pixels darker than it become black, and lighter pixels become white. That simplification is useful for scanned signatures, pencil sketches, stamps, diagrams and text that will be printed at small sizes. Adjust the slider while watching the preview, because a cut-off that is too high thickens lines and fills fine gaps, while one that is too low drops faint strokes. Threshold is not a substitute for a scanner's descreening; moire patterns from printed halftones can survive. For a high-contrast line art effect, start with a clean, evenly lit scan and then fine-tune the slider. Test the slider on a small crop before processing a whole page.

article.heading: Transparency and export formats
paragraphs: Transparency is preserved in both modes. The alpha channel is left alone, so a cut-out on a transparent background keeps its soft edges and a product photo does not gain a white rectangle. To keep that transparency, download PNG or WebP. JPG stores no alpha information, so any transparent area is flattened, usually to white or black. PNG is the safest choice for logos and overlays; WebP gives smaller files for web use; JPG is fine when the background is already solid. Re-encoding always writes new pixels, so export once from the version you are happy with instead of repeatedly downloading and reopening the same file. Keep a lossless master copy if you plan several exports.

article.heading: A quick conversion workflow
paragraphs: Start by opening a PNG, JPG or WebP file from your device. Choose Grayscale for a photograph or Threshold for artwork that needs crisp edges. In threshold mode, move the slider in small steps and watch thin lines and empty spaces; stop when the drawing reads cleanly at the size you plan to use it. Zoom the preview to catch broken strokes before downloading. If the image has a transparent background, confirm it still looks transparent in the preview, then pick a format that supports alpha. Download the file, give it a clear name and compare it with the original. If the result is too heavy or too large for a web page, resize or compress it afterwards.

article.heading: Limits and troubleshooting
paragraphs: This tool changes tone, not content. It cannot colorise an old photograph, repair scratches, straighten a skewed page or add missing detail to a low-resolution scan. Very large images need more memory and may take a few seconds to update, especially in threshold mode where every pixel is examined again. If the preview appears blank or unchanged, check that the file actually opened and that a supported format was used. Noisy results usually come from JPEG compression or uneven lighting; a cleaner source gives a cleaner cut-off. All processing is local, but remember that clipboard screenshots, shared screens and downloaded files can still expose an image you intended to keep private. If a file will not open, try re-saving it from the source application.

name: Image Flip & Rotate
title: Image Flip & Rotate — Mirror and Turn Photos in 90° Steps
description: Flip or rotate images in your browser. Mirror horizontally or vertically, turn in 90-degree steps, combine operations, and export PNG, JPG or WebP without upload.
intro: Mirror a photo left to right or top to bottom, and rotate it in quarter turns. Operations can be combined in any order, and the result keeps the same pixel count apart from the width and height swap caused by odd quarter turns. Everything runs locally and downloads as PNG, JPG or WebP.
instructions: Open a PNG, JPG or WebP image from your device.
Choose horizontal or vertical flip to mirror the picture.
Rotate clockwise or counterclockwise in 90-degree steps.
Combine flips and turns until the orientation looks right.
Download the corrected image as PNG, JPG or WebP.

example.input: A sideways photo of a person
example.output: The same photo turned 90 degrees and mirrored horizontally, saved as JPG

faqs.q: Does the photo leave my device?
faqs.a: No. Flipping and rotating are done in your browser with the file you open. Nothing is uploaded, and the image is discarded when the page is closed.

faqs.q: Does rotating reduce image quality?
faqs.a: A 90-degree rotation is a pixel rearrangement, so the rotation itself loses no detail. Quality can change when the result is encoded to JPG, which is lossy, or resized. Choose PNG or WebP to avoid JPG re-encoding artifacts.

faqs.q: Can I rotate by any angle, such as 17 degrees?
faqs.a: No. This tool turns images in 90-degree increments only. It does not do free-angle rotation, perspective correction or straightening of a tilted horizon.

faqs.q: Will camera orientation metadata be handled?
faqs.a: The preview uses the pixels as opened. The exported file is a fresh image without the original rotation tag, so check the visible result before downloading instead of relying on metadata.

faqs.q: Why does my export look blank or still sideways?
faqs.a: Very large files can take time to draw, so wait for the preview before downloading. If the photo still appears sideways, confirm you applied a quarter turn rather than a mirror, and open the downloaded file instead of a cached thumbnail.

article.heading: What flipping and rotating change
paragraphs: Flipping and rotating are orientation fixes, not content edits. A flip mirrors the picture across an axis, while a rotation moves every pixel around the centre. This tool performs both locally: you open a file, choose the operations, watch the preview and download a new image. It is useful for photos from phones, scanned pages, screenshots and design assets that arrived the wrong way round. Because the work happens in the browser, there is no upload and no waiting for a remote service. The controls are deliberately simple, so you can correct orientation in a few clicks without opening a full image editor or learning layers, masks and selection tools. Undoing a step is as simple as pressing the opposite control.

article.heading: Quarter turns and dimension swaps
paragraphs: A quarter turn moves the top edge to the side, so 90 and 270 degree results swap the width and height of the canvas. Two turns give a 180 degree result and keep the original dimensions. Each step is exact: there is no interpolation and no resampling, so the number of pixels stays the same and edges remain sharp. You can turn clockwise or counterclockwise and apply as many steps as you need, because four quarter turns return the image to its starting orientation. Watch the preview after each click; if you overshoot, keep turning rather than trying to undo a resizing operation elsewhere. Keep track of the count if you plan to return to the original angle.

article.heading: Horizontal and vertical mirrors
paragraphs: A horizontal flip mirrors left and right, which is handy for fixing selfies saved backwards or matching a logo that faces the other way. A vertical flip mirrors top and bottom, useful when a scan or a texture came out inverted. Mirrors do not swap canvas dimensions. Text becomes reversed, so a flipped screenshot will no longer read correctly; that is expected behaviour rather than a bug. If you are preparing a design element, check that any lettering, arrows or logos still face the intended direction before you download. For photographs without text, a mirror is often the quickest way to fix composition. Mirroring twice in the same direction simply restores the first view. Check the edges of the frame as well as the centre.

article.heading: Combining operations
paragraphs: Flips and turns can be combined in any order. A photo that is upside down and mirrored can be corrected with one quarter turn and one horizontal flip. The controls apply each operation to the current preview, so stacking them works naturally and you can keep clicking until the orientation is right. There is no history list here, so if you go too far, repeat the opposite operation or reopen the source file and start again. Combine orientation fixes before other edits: once you crop or resize, the relationship between edges changes and it becomes harder to judge which way is up. Write down the sequence you used so you can repeat it on similar photos.

article.heading: Formats and image quality
paragraphs: Downloads are available as PNG, JPG or WebP. PNG keeps lossless pixels and transparency, WebP gives smaller files while supporting transparency, and JPG is widely compatible but uses lossy compression. A 90 degree rotation only rearranges existing pixels, so the rotation itself does not soften the picture. Any change in sharpness comes from re-encoding, especially when saving a PNG as JPG, or from later resizing. To keep the best quality, export once in the format you need and avoid repeatedly opening and saving the same file. Check the preview at full size before downloading a large photo. A downloaded JPG cannot later be turned back into the exact PNG you started with. Choose the format before you leave the page.

article.heading: Limits, privacy and fixes
paragraphs: This tool does not rotate by arbitrary angles, straighten a tilted horizon, crop edges or correct perspective. It also does not edit camera orientation tags; it writes a fresh image from the pixels you see, so an exported file should look correct without depending on metadata. All processing is local and nothing is uploaded, although a shared screen or a file left in a download folder can still reveal an image you meant to keep private. If a preview looks blank, wait for a large file to finish decoding, then try a smaller copy. If the result still appears sideways, confirm you applied a turn rather than a mirror and open the downloaded file directly.

name: Image Resizer
title: Image Resizer — Set Exact Width and Height in Pixels
description: Resize photos to exact pixel dimensions. Lock aspect ratio, use fit or stretch modes within a documented pixel cap, and export PNG, JPG or WebP.
intro: Set an exact pixel width and height for any PNG, JPG or WebP image. Keep the aspect ratio locked for proportional resizing, or turn it off to fit or stretch the picture into the requested box. Dimensions are capped at a documented maximum to keep the browser responsive.
instructions: Open a PNG, JPG or WebP image from your device.
Enter the target width and height in pixels.
Keep aspect ratio locked to scale proportionally, or unlock it for an exact box.
Choose Fit to contain the image or Stretch to fill the dimensions.
Review the preview and download as PNG, JPG or WebP.

example.output: A 600 by 400 PNG scaled proportionally with the aspect ratio locked

faqs.q: Is my image uploaded to resize it?
faqs.a: No. The resizing happens in your browser using the file you open. No copy is sent to a server, and the working image is cleared when the page closes.

faqs.q: What is the maximum output size?
faqs.a: Width and height are each capped at a documented limit to protect browser memory. Requests above that limit show a clear error; for a larger result, use a desktop editor or work in stages.

faqs.q: What happens when I unlock the aspect ratio?
faqs.a: Unlocked mode lets you set any width and height. Fit scales the image to stay inside that box, which can leave empty space, while Stretch changes the proportions to fill it exactly and may distort faces or circles.

faqs.q: Can I enlarge a small photo without blur?
faqs.a: You can enter dimensions larger than the source, but the browser can only interpolate existing pixels. Upscaling looks soft and cannot create new detail that was never captured.

faqs.q: Why did my download keep the original size?
faqs.a: Check that you applied the resize before downloading and that both values are positive numbers within the allowed cap. A very large source may take time to process, so wait for the preview to update. Reloading also resets settings.

article.heading: What resizing actually does
paragraphs: Resizing changes the number of pixels in an image rather than cropping its content. You supply a target width and height, and the tool draws the source at that size, then writes a new file. This is useful for preparing avatars, product photos, email signatures, web headers and screenshots that must meet fixed dimension rules. Everything happens in your browser: the file you open is decoded locally, the new pixels are calculated locally, and only the finished download leaves the page. No account, upload queue or remote processing is involved. The preview lets you compare the new size with the original before you commit to a download. You can repeat the process with different values until the preview looks right.

article.heading: Entering exact dimensions
paragraphs: Width and height are entered as whole pixel values. The original dimensions are shown so you can scale by a known factor, for example halving a 1600 by 1200 photo to 800 by 600. With the aspect ratio locked, changing one field updates the other to keep the same proportions. That is the safest option for photographs because it avoids squashed faces and oval circles. If you need an exact canvas size, unlock the ratio and enter both values. Remember that a resize changes pixels, not the framing: the whole picture is kept, so a wide photo placed in a narrow box is scaled down rather than cropped. Write down the original dimensions if you may need to restore them later.

article.heading: Aspect ratio lock, fit and stretch
paragraphs: When the aspect ratio is locked, the image scales proportionally to the requested width or height. When it is unlocked, two modes decide how the picture fills the target box. Fit scales the image as large as possible while keeping every edge inside the dimensions, which may leave unused space along one side. Stretch maps the source directly onto the requested width and height, filling the box but changing proportions if they differ from the original. Use Fit for layouts where empty space is acceptable and Stretch only when a slight distortion is harmless, such as a background texture. Check the preview at both settings before deciding. A narrow column or a wide banner often needs different choices.

article.heading: Formats and quality trade-offs
paragraphs: The download can be saved as PNG, JPG or WebP. PNG keeps pixels lossless and preserves transparency, which matters for logos and cut-outs. JPG is compact and widely supported but discards detail on each save, so use it for photographs without transparent areas. WebP offers smaller files with transparency support. Resizing itself interpolates pixels, and encoding can add further change, especially when the source is PNG and the output is JPG. Export once from the version you like instead of resizing repeatedly, because each round adds another generation of compression. Match the format to where the image will be used. Transparent areas also need a format that can store them. Check the file size after each export.

article.heading: Upscaling and the pixel cap
paragraphs: You can enter values larger than the source, but enlargement cannot invent detail. The browser fills in new pixels by interpolating nearby ones, so an upscaled photo looks soft and may show visible blocks at high zoom. A small icon enlarged to a banner will rarely look sharp. Downscaling usually looks better, particularly when the source has plenty of detail. To keep output manageable, width and height are each capped at a documented maximum; requests above that limit are rejected with a clear message. If you genuinely need a huge print, use a dedicated desktop editor rather than stacking browser resizes. The cap is shown in the tool so you know the limit before you start.

article.heading: Workflow, privacy and fixes
paragraphs: Open an image, enter the target size, choose the ratio and fill mode, then review the preview before downloading. Names and settings are not saved after the page closes, so a reload resets the tool. No image data is uploaded, but a shared screen, clipboard or download folder can still expose a private picture. If nothing happens after you click download, confirm both dimensions are positive numbers and within the cap, and wait for a large source to finish drawing. If the result looks distorted, re-lock the aspect ratio or switch from Stretch to Fit. If the file appears unchanged, check that you are opening the downloaded version rather than the original thumbnail.

name: Image to SVG
title: Image to SVG — Wrap a Raster Picture in SVG Markup
description: Wrap a PNG, JPG or WebP image in an SVG using a Base64 data URL. It includes width and height metadata and downloads as .svg, but does not vector-trace.
intro: Embed a raster picture inside an SVG document by encoding it as a Base64 data URL in an image element. The exported .svg file carries the source width and height as metadata and displays the same pixels as the original. It is a wrapper, not a vector trace.
instructions: Open a PNG, JPG or WebP image from your device.
Review the detected width and height shown for the source.
Note that the SVG embeds the original pixels rather than redrawing them as paths.
Download the generated .svg file.
Open the SVG in a browser or place it in your HTML to check the result.

example.output: An SVG file with an image element holding a Base64 data URL and 200 by 200 metadata

faqs.q: Is my image sent to a server?
faqs.a: No. The file is read in your browser and encoded to a Base64 data URL locally. Nothing is uploaded, and the encoded copy exists only in the current page until you download it.

faqs.q: Can I edit the lines after conversion?
faqs.a: No. The SVG contains an image element pointing to the original raster data, not vector paths. There are no nodes or curves to move, so zooming reveals the same pixels as the source.

faqs.q: Will it stay sharp at any size?
faqs.a: No. Because the pixels are embedded rather than redrawn, enlarging the SVG enlarges the same raster image. For truly resolution-independent artwork, use a tracing tool or redraw the graphic with shapes.

faqs.q: Why is the SVG bigger than the original image?
faqs.a: Base64 expands binary data by about one third, so the embedded copy is larger than the source file. A 1 MB PNG produces an SVG of roughly 1.3 MB before the added markup.

faqs.q: Why does my SVG show a blank box in some apps?
faqs.a: Some older editors do not render data URLs inside image elements. Open the file in a browser first to confirm it is valid. If a tool strips the data URL, link to a separate image file instead, though that loses the single-file convenience.

article.heading: What this conversion does
paragraphs: An SVG is normally associated with shapes, paths and text that stay sharp at any size. This tool takes a different approach: it places your existing raster picture inside an SVG document as an image element. The pixels are not redrawn or traced; they are carried along unchanged. The result is a single .svg file that browsers can display like any other vector document, with the source width and height recorded in the markup. Understanding that difference matters, because the file is a convenient wrapper rather than a vector version of your artwork, and it will behave like the original photo when scaled. A browser treats that wrapper much like any other SVG file. The markup stays small and easy to inspect.

article.heading: How the Base64 data URL works
paragraphs: To keep the picture inside one file, the source bytes are encoded as Base64 text and written into the href of an SVG image element using a data URL. Base64 maps binary data to printable characters, which makes it safe to store inside an XML attribute. The browser decodes that text back into the original image when it renders the document. Because the encoding is reversible, the embedded picture is identical to what you opened; no quality is gained or lost in the conversion step. The trade-off is size: the text form is about one third larger than the binary file it represents. The same bytes come out when a browser decodes the attribute. No hidden service performs the encoding for you.

article.heading: What is inside the exported file
paragraphs: The exported document is small and readable. It contains an opening svg tag with width and height attributes taken from the source image, a viewBox that matches those dimensions, and a single image element whose href holds the data URL. There are no layers, paths, gradients or filters. That simplicity is useful when you want a self-contained asset that can be dropped into HTML, stored in a content system that accepts SVG, or referenced from CSS without a separate image request. You can open the file in a text editor to inspect the metadata, but editing the encoded string by hand is rarely helpful. That makes the file easy to version-control alongside your source code.

article.heading: Formats and size implications
paragraphs: Open a PNG, JPG or WebP image, check the detected dimensions, and download the generated file. PNG is a good source when transparency matters, because the alpha channel survives inside the embedded data. JPG is smaller for photographs but has no transparency. WebP is compact and widely supported in browsers. In every case the SVG simply carries the bytes you supplied, so its visual quality is exactly the source quality. If you later need a different size, resize the source image first and convert again; editing the width attribute alone only stretches the same pixels. Keep the original image file as well, because it is easier to re-edit. Check that the chosen format supports any transparency you need.

article.heading: When this approach is useful
paragraphs: A wrapped SVG is handy when a platform accepts SVG uploads but not image files, when you want one self-contained asset with no external references, or when an icon system expects SVG markup. It is also a quick way to include a raster picture in an SVG-based layout without managing a second file. It is not useful when you need to change individual shapes, recolour parts of a drawing, print at billboard size or minimise file size. For those jobs, redraw the artwork with vector tools or run a tracing conversion that produces real paths from the pixel edges. It is also a poor choice when bandwidth matters, since Base64 adds overhead. Think of it as packaging, not artwork conversion.

article.heading: Limits, privacy and troubleshooting
paragraphs: This conversion does not vector-trace, remove backgrounds, sharpen, compress or alter the picture. Enlarging the SVG reveals the same detail and blur as enlarging the original raster file, so it is not resolution-independent. Encoding is local: the image never leaves your browser, and the downloaded file contains only your data. Some design applications do not render data URLs in SVG image elements; if you see an empty box, open the file in a browser to confirm it is valid, then use a linked image instead for that application. Very large photos create large SVGs and may take a moment to encode. A large photo may also make the markup slow to copy into an editor.

name: Image Inverter
title: Image Inverter — Reverse RGB Colours into a Negative
description: Reverse every RGB channel value directly in your browser to create negative artwork, then export the result as PNG, JPG or WebP with transparency preserved.
intro: Image Inverter subtracts each red, green and blue channel from 255, turning light areas dark and dark areas light. Transparent pixels keep their alpha, so cut-outs and overlays stay usable. This is a creative colour effect, not a photographic exposure correction.
instructions: Open a PNG, JPG or WebP image from your device.
Review the live negative preview; transparency is kept unchanged.
Export as PNG for alpha, JPG for small photos or WebP for a modern balance.
Download the result and compare it with the original before reuse.

example.input: A blue circle on a white background with transparent corners.
example.output: A yellow circle on a black background with unchanged transparent corners.

faqs.q: Is my image uploaded to a server?
faqs.a: No. The file is decoded and its pixels are changed in your browser only. Nothing is sent to LetitEdit or to a separate image-processing service.

faqs.q: Does this repair an underexposed photograph?
faqs.a: No. Inversion simply maps each RGB value to its opposite. It cannot recover shadow detail, correct white balance or replace proper photo editing, so treat the result as a stylised negative.

faqs.q: What happens to transparent pixels?
faqs.a: The alpha channel is left exactly as it was. Only red, green and blue values are reversed, so semi-transparent edges and cut-outs keep their original shape and opacity.

faqs.q: Which export format should I choose?
faqs.a: PNG keeps alpha and avoids extra compression artefacts. JPG cannot store transparency, so it flattens those pixels, while WebP can keep alpha and often produces a smaller file.

faqs.q: Why does a JPG export look different from the preview?
faqs.a: JPG compression changes pixel values and removes transparency. If the difference matters, download PNG or WebP instead, then compare the result with the on-screen preview.

article.heading: How the inversion works
paragraphs: Image Inverter reads the pixel data of your picture and replaces each red, green and blue value with 255 minus that value. A white pixel becomes black, a black pixel becomes white, and a mid-grey pixel stays close to the same brightness because its channels are already near the centre of the range. A blue area turns yellow because its red and green channels rise while its blue channel falls. The calculation is applied to every pixel independently, so the effect is fast, predictable and easy to understand. It is a mathematical colour flip rather than an analysis of the subject matter in the picture. Because the operation is uniform, the same input always produces the same output and there is no hidden adjustment based on subject or colour space.

article.heading: Why transparency survives
paragraphs: A pixel in a browser canvas has four channels: red, green, blue and alpha. The first three describe colour, while alpha describes opacity. This tool changes only the colour channels and leaves alpha untouched. That means a transparent corner stays transparent, and a half-faded shadow keeps the same degree of fade. This detail matters when you invert a logo, icon or cut-out that will sit on top of another design. If the alpha channel were flipped as well, solid areas could vanish and empty areas could become opaque, destroying the silhouette. Keeping alpha separate makes the result useful as a layer rather than just a flat picture. This also makes it safe to composite the inverted layer over a different background after export instead of being locked to the original canvas colour.

article.heading: When the effect is useful
paragraphs: Negative colours are popular for posters, album covers, game sprites and playful social graphics. The strong contrast can make simple shapes feel fresh without redrawing them. Designers also use inversion when exploring dark mode artwork, because it quickly suggests how light backgrounds and bright accents might read against a darker palette. Inverted text can create a striking label or sticker, although it should be checked for legibility at final size. Science and craft projects may use the same effect to discuss how light and colour are represented digitally. In each case, the value is in the immediate visual change, not in any hidden interpretation of the image. Try it on line art, simple icons and bold typography first, where the channel flip is easy to judge before you apply it to a complex composition.

article.heading: What it cannot repair
paragraphs: It is important to separate a negative effect from photographic correction. Inverting a dim photo will not reveal faces hidden in shadow, remove a colour cast or recover clipped highlights. Those problems need exposure controls, curves, local adjustments or a better original capture. This tool also does not detect edges, isolate objects or apply a film look; it simply reverses channel values. If you want a monochrome finish, a black-and-white converter is a better starting point. If you need a gentler design change, try resizing, rotating or adding a border instead. Knowing the narrow purpose prevents disappointment and helps you choose the right companion tool. For a subtle result, make a duplicate, invert only part of the design or combine the effect with a monochrome pass rather than treating it as a final edit.

article.heading: Exporting and troubleshooting
paragraphs: PNG is the safest download when transparency matters, because it stores alpha without forcing the image into a lossy format. JPG produces small files for photographs but flattens transparency and can soften sharp edges. WebP offers a modern compromise and can carry alpha, although very old software may not open it. If an export looks different from the preview, check the chosen format first and switch to PNG for a faithful result. Very large pictures may take a moment to decode in any browser, so wait for the preview to update before downloading. Your image stays on your device throughout the process. If colours look unexpected, remember that complementary values are produced channel by channel; a red region turns cyan, while a green region turns magenta.

name: Image to Text (OCR)
title: Image to Text (OCR) — English Extraction in Your Browser
description: Extract English text from images with a locally loaded Tesseract.js OCR engine and language data; nothing is uploaded, and you can copy or download the result.
intro: This tool loads a Tesseract.js worker and English language data with the page, then decodes your image in the browser and runs recognition locally. A progress indicator shows loading and recognition, and the output is the real extracted text rather than a demonstration string. Copy it or download a .txt file when the result looks right.
instructions: Wait for the OCR worker and English data to finish loading.
Choose a clear PNG, JPG or WebP image containing printed English text.
Start recognition and watch the progress indicator.
Review the extracted text for spacing and punctuation errors.
Copy the text or download it as a .txt file.

example.input: A sharp photo of a printed sign that says OPEN TODAY.
example.output: Recognised text: OPEN TODAY, ready to copy or save as .txt.

faqs.q: Does my image get uploaded for recognition?
faqs.a: No. The image is decoded in your browser and passed to a locally loaded Tesseract.js worker. The page must download the worker and WASM files with its other assets, but your image bytes are not sent to LetitEdit or an outside OCR service.

faqs.q: Why is this build English only?
faqs.a: It loads English language data, so it recognises printed English characters and words. Other scripts and languages are outside this build and may produce poor or empty results even when the image itself is clear.

faqs.q: What affects recognition accuracy?
faqs.a: Font, size, contrast and language all matter. Sharp, evenly lit images with generous spacing usually work best, while blur, glare, low contrast, decorative fonts and angled text increase mistakes. Handwriting is unreliable.

faqs.q: Why did the worker fail to start?
faqs.a: The OCR engine needs its worker and WASM download with the page. If those files are blocked, cached incorrectly or unavailable offline, recognition cannot begin. Reload the page, allow the files to load, then try again.

faqs.q: Can I trust the text without checking it?
faqs.a: Always review it. The output shown is genuinely extracted text with copy and .txt download controls, but OCR can confuse similar characters, spacing and punctuation. Compare important names, numbers and links with the original image before using them.

article.heading: What the OCR engine does
paragraphs: Optical character recognition looks for shapes in an image that match letters, numbers and punctuation, then assembles them into words. This tool uses a Tesseract.js engine loaded locally alongside the page, together with English language data that helps the recogniser choose between similar possibilities. The image is decoded into pixels in your browser before recognition starts. A progress indicator reports the loading and recognition stages, so you can see whether the engine is preparing, working or finished. When it stops, the panel contains the real text that the engine found, ready for review rather than a prewritten placeholder. The recogniser returns a plain text block rather than a formatted document, so line breaks, columns and table structure may need cleanup in your own editor afterwards.

article.heading: Where your image goes
paragraphs: Privacy is straightforward here: the picture stays in your browser. Recognition runs in a worker, which is a separate script thread that keeps the page responsive while it processes pixels. The worker and its WASM support files have to be downloaded with the page, just as any other engine asset would be. That download is not an upload of your document. No photo, screenshot or scan is posted to a server by this tool. Once you close or refresh the page, the in-memory image is gone. You still control what happens next, because the extracted text is only copied or downloaded when you choose to do so. If you close the tab during a run, the session ends and you will need to choose the image and start again.

article.heading: What changes accuracy
paragraphs: Recognition quality depends heavily on the source image. A large, sharp picture with dark printed letters on a plain light background usually gives clean results. Small fonts, fuzzy focus, glare, shadows, low contrast and decorative typefaces can turn one character into another or split words incorrectly. Angled pages are harder than flat ones, and dense tables may be read in the wrong order. Language is a hard limit as well: this build loads English data only, so other scripts are not reliably supported. Handwriting and stylised lettering remain difficult for OCR generally. A few minutes spent preparing a clearer image often improves the result more than repeated recognition attempts. Cropping tightly around the text and resizing a small scan to a clearer size are simple ways to reduce those errors before another attempt.

article.heading: Reading the result critically
paragraphs: OCR produces text, not a guarantee. The panel may include every word correctly, or it may swap similar letters, add stray spaces, miss punctuation or join two lines together. Treat the result as a draft that you inspect against the original picture. Pay particular attention to proper names, numbers, dates, amounts and links, since a single mistaken character can change their meaning. When the text looks right, use the copy button to paste it elsewhere or download it as a plain .txt file. That file contains only the extracted text, which makes it convenient for notes, spreadsheets, accessibility checks and search indexes after you have made any needed corrections. The download keeps the spelling exactly as recognised, so make corrections in your own document if you plan to publish or share the content widely.

article.heading: Troubleshooting common failures
paragraphs: If the engine never reaches recognition, check that the worker and WASM files loaded with the page. Network filtering, an interrupted refresh or offline use can prevent them from arriving, and reloading usually fixes the problem. If recognition runs but returns little or nothing, inspect the image: crop away clutter, straighten the page, increase contrast or use a sharper source. Very large images can be slow to decode, so a moderate resized copy may work better. Remember that English-only language data cannot solve a page written in another language. After any retry, compare the new output with the original instead of assuming that a longer result is automatically a more accurate one. A second try with a better crop is usually faster than manually fixing dozens of uncertain characters in the output.

name: QR Code Generator
title: QR Code Generator — Text, URLs and Image Codes
description: Create QR codes for text or URLs in your browser, choose error correction, size and colours, then download PNG or SVG after a quick scan test.
intro: QR Code Generator turns text or a URL into a scannable image without sending the content to a server. You can change error correction, module size and colours to suit a screen, poster or label. In image mode, the private picture is converted to a data URL and embedded only when it fits the QR capacity; otherwise the tool explains why and asks for a hosted public URL, and LetitEdit never uploads the private image.
instructions: Choose text, URL or image mode and enter the content.
Pick an error-correction level and set the size and colours.
For image mode, confirm the data URL fits or provide a hosted public URL.
Preview the QR code and scan it with your phone.
Download PNG for bitmaps or SVG for scalable printing.

example.input: A URL with medium error correction, dark navy modules and a 512 px size.
example.output: A scannable QR PNG or SVG that opens that URL when tested with a phone.

faqs.q: Does LetitEdit upload my private image?
faqs.a: No. Image mode converts your picture to a data URL and embeds that text only if it fits the code. If it does not fit, the tool shows a clear error and asks you to supply a hosted public URL. LetitEdit never uploads the private image.

faqs.q: Why was my image rejected in image mode?
faqs.a: A QR code has limited capacity. An embedded data URL can exceed that limit, especially for a large or detailed picture. When this happens, the page explains the problem and asks for a public hosted URL instead; it will not silently shrink or upload your file.

faqs.q: What do error-correction levels change?
faqs.a: Higher levels let a scanner recover data when part of the code is dirty, damaged or covered, but they leave less room for the actual content. Lower levels store more data and are suitable when the printed code will stay clean and unobstructed.

faqs.q: Should I download PNG or SVG?
faqs.a: PNG is a bitmap that suits screens and simple printing. SVG keeps the modules as vectors, so they stay crisp when enlarged for posters or labels. In both cases, scan-test the finished code before printing a large batch.

faqs.q: Why will my QR code not scan?
faqs.a: Common causes are a very small size, weak contrast between modules and background, inverted or unusual colours, glare on a screen and a pattern placed too close to the edge. Increase the size, restore strong contrast, choose a suitable error-correction level and test with a phone.

article.heading: How the code is made
paragraphs: A QR code stores content as a grid of dark and light modules that a camera can interpret. This generator builds that grid in your browser from the text, URL or image content you provide. You can choose how much error correction to reserve, adjust the overall size and change the module and background colours for a particular design. The preview updates so you can see the pattern before downloading anything. Nothing about your input needs to leave the page for the mathematics to work. The result is an image file containing the code, which you can place in a document, on a screen or on printed material after checking that it scans.

article.heading: The error-correction trade-off
paragraphs: Error correction is one of the most useful controls in a QR generator. Extra redundancy is added to the code so a scanner can still recover the message if a corner is scratched, a label is slightly obscured or printing is imperfect. The trade-off is capacity: a higher level spends more modules on recovery information and leaves fewer for your content. A short URL can usually tolerate a strong level, while a long paragraph or embedded data may need a lower one. If the code will appear on a clean screen, a modest level is often enough. For packaging, signs or outdoor labels, choose more protection and test the final version.

article.heading: Image mode and capacity
paragraphs: Image mode is deliberately conservative. Your picture is turned into a data URL, which is a text form of the image bytes, and that text is offered as the QR payload. The tool checks whether the data fits the selected code capacity. If it fits, the image is embedded without an upload. If it does not fit, you get a clear error asking for a hosted public URL rather than a mysterious blank preview. LetitEdit never uploads your private image on your behalf. Supplying a hosted URL means you choose where the picture lives and whether that address is public, which keeps the privacy decision with you.

article.heading: Choosing a download
paragraphs: PNG is the straightforward choice for web pages, presentations and app screenshots because it is a familiar bitmap format. SVG stores the pattern as shapes, so it remains sharp at any print size and is useful for posters, labels and vinyl cutters. Custom colours can make a code fit a brand palette, but the contrast between modules and background must stay strong. Very light yellows, pale greys or similar tones can confuse cameras. Leave clear space around the pattern when you place it, and avoid stretching the exported file unevenly. Before printing many copies, scan a sample with more than one phone to catch display and camera differences.

article.heading: Privacy and practical checks
paragraphs: Every part of generation happens in the browser, including encoding, customisation and download. A QR code is only a picture of the content you enter, so anyone who scans it will see that content. Do not encode private notes, passwords or confidential links just because generation is local. For plain text and URLs, check that the spelling and destination are correct before exporting. For image mode, remember that a hosted public URL must remain available for as long as the code is useful. Scan the final PNG or SVG in the size and colours you intend to publish, especially before printing, because a code that looks fine on screen can fail when reproduced poorly.

article.heading: Common mistakes to avoid
paragraphs: Most scanning failures come from presentation rather than encoding. A code printed too small for the camera to resolve, placed on a busy background, or surrounded by a cropped edge is harder to read than one with generous quiet space. Inverted colours can work in specialist software but often fail in ordinary camera apps, so keep dark modules on a light field unless you have tested the reverse. Short links are easier to fit and usually scan faster than long tracking URLs with many query parameters. If you need to change the destination later, remember that a printed code cannot be edited; consider linking to a stable page that you control instead of a temporary campaign address.

name: Image Compressor
title: Image Compressor — Reduce JPG, WebP and PNG Size
description: Re-encode images through a canvas with selectable JPEG or WebP quality and an optional maximum dimension, comparing original and resulting byte sizes before download.
intro: Image Compressor redraws your picture on a canvas and encodes it again at the quality you choose. You can cap the longest edge, compare the original and resulting byte sizes, and download the smaller file. PNG is re-encoded losslessly, so quality has no effect, and your file stays in the browser with very large inputs rejected by a clear limit.
instructions: Choose a PNG, JPG or WebP file within the stated size limit.
Select the output format and, for JPEG or WebP, set a quality level.
Optionally enter a maximum dimension to scale the longest edge.
Compare the original and resulting byte sizes shown below the preview.
Download the compressed image if the trade-off looks acceptable.

example.input: A 12 MB JPEG photo with quality set to 0.75 and a 1600 px maximum edge.
example.output: A smaller JPEG whose byte size is shown beside the original 12 MB figure.

faqs.q: Is my image uploaded for compression?
faqs.a: No. The file is decoded, drawn to a canvas and encoded again in your browser. Nothing is sent to LetitEdit or to an external compression service.

faqs.q: Why does the quality setting not change my PNG?
faqs.a: PNG is lossless, so quality does not apply. The setting affects JPEG and WebP output only. To reduce a PNG, try the maximum dimension control or switch to WebP when that format is acceptable.

faqs.q: Why was my file rejected?
faqs.a: Very large files are refused so the page stays responsive and your browser does not run out of memory. The page states the size limit clearly. Resize or trim the original before choosing it again.

faqs.q: Will a lower quality always produce a smaller file?
